THE BUSINESS 100 · METHODOLOGY

How we count the value

Each company on the list creates value for many people at once: owners, workers, governments, partners and customers. We show that value through separate lenses, each with its own source and caveats, and we show how every number was reached.

Value createdThe lensesPaid outEvidenceWhat we don’t countCoverage

What “value created” means here

“Value created” is the umbrella. Under it sit separate lenses: market value, the people a company employs and what they earn, what it paid out to others, who owns it, the cash it returns, what flows through its platform, the taxes it pays and what it spends on research.

Lenses are not added to each other or to market value. They measure different things, in different units and sometimes different years, and they overlap. A worker’s pay funds income taxes. A seller’s sales on a platform are also that seller’s revenue. Adding them would count the same dollar more than once.

One measure combines figures on purpose: paid out & sales enabled. It adds up the parts of what a company paid to others, which don’t overlap with each other, and for marketplaces the sales its platform made for others. It never adds estimated pay (which is already inside it), market value or any other lens. And it is never totaled across the list, because one company’s payment is another company’s revenue.

The lenses

Ranking figures (market value, people employed and estimated pay) come from the list’s 2024–25 snapshot. Everything else comes from each company’s own filings for the fiscal year that matches the snapshot, with a verbatim quote of the line it came from.

Value created (market value)

What it is
Market capitalization at year-end 2024: shares outstanding × share price. It is what the company’s owners hold.
Source
CompaniesMarketCap, linked on every profile.
Caveats
A snapshot of equity value that moves with the share price. It leaves out what customers, workers and partners gained. Many people built each company; each profile highlights one leader.

People employed

What it is
Direct employees of the company and its subsidiaries, including through acquisitions.
Source
Annual reports and Stock Analysis, generally for fiscal 2024 or the first half of 2025.
Caveats
Where reporting overlaps, some people may be counted twice. Contractors and suppliers’ workers are not included.

Estimated pay

What it is
People employed × an assumed yearly pay per person in USD, set by industry and in some cases home country.
Source
Our estimate. Each profile shows the assumption and lets you move it 25% either way.
Caveats
Not a reported figure. Actual pay varies by role and location.

Paid out & sales enabled

What it is
The money a company paid other people and businesses in one fiscal year: employees, suppliers, partners, lenders and governments, plus builders and equipment makers for its capital spending. For marketplaces only (Shopify, Uber, Airbnb, eBay, MercadoLibre and Grab), it adds the sales the platform enabled for others. The ranking shows it in USD.
Formula
Paid out = revenue − operating cash flow + capital spending, plus interest paid and income taxes paid only where the company reports them outside operating cash flow. Operating cash flow is what is left of customers’ payments after the company has paid its employees, suppliers, partners, lenders and governments, so revenue minus operating cash flow is what it paid all of them. Capital spending is purchases of property, equipment and intangible assets, excluding acquisitions and vehicles or equipment bought to lease to customers. Sales enabled = the marketplace’s own gross volume (GMV, gross bookings or gross booking value) − its revenue, minus its own first-party sales where it states them.
Customer lending
Some companies book growth in customer loans, lease fleets or finance receivables inside operating cash flow (carmakers’ finance arms, for example). That growth is lending, not a payment. Where the company discloses the amount, we show paid out adjusted for it and rank that figure; the profile keeps both numbers. Where it doesn’t, paid out is shown unadjusted with a caveat.
How we checked it
In a pilot on eight companies, the formula’s payments to suppliers and employees came within 0.5% of the figures Biocon publishes in its own statement of economic value distributed, and the formula agreed within ±3% of a cost-based calculation at six of the eight. Our build recomputes every figure from its inputs and stops if a stored figure disagrees.
Source
The income statement and cash-flow statement in the company’s 10-K, 20-F or annual report, each input with a verbatim quote; the marketplace volumes come from the Ecosystem lens. Non-USD figures are converted at the Federal Reserve’s annual average exchange rate (G.5A) for the calendar year that covers most of the fiscal year; profiles show the native currency.
Not counted
Payment volume, client assets and studies a company commissioned are never used as sales enabled. Dividends and buybacks are not payouts here: they are financing flows, shown in Cash to shareholders.
Not comparable
Banks and brokers: their cash flows are mostly customers’ deposits and loans, so the formula doesn’t apply. Their profiles show operating costs paid, excluding interest (noninterest expense − depreciation and amortization − stock-based compensation + income taxes paid), with interest paid to depositors and lenders beside it, never added. They sort last in the column.
Caveats
One fiscal year: working-capital swings move it, and a company that builds inventory or spends heavily on capital projects can pay out more than its revenue. Interest and dividends received inside operating cash flow lower it; non-cash revenue raises it. Payments companies, exchanges and asset managers use the formula with a sector flag. Insurance-heavy Berkshire Hathaway counts claims paid as payouts. Sales enabled is the value of others’ sales, not their earnings. Estimated pay to workers is already inside paid out and is never added to it, and the column is never summed across companies.

Ownership

What it is
Who holds the company’s shares, as a percentage of all shares outstanding (economic ownership, not votes). Voting power is shown separately when a filing states it.
Source
Proxy statements, annual reports, 20-F and 40-F filings, Schedules 13D and 13G, and exchange shareholding disclosures.
Who stands behind everyone else
Named holders that are index funds and asset managers are grouped together, each with who it invests for in its own words. Norway’s Government Pension Fund Global (from NBIM’s year-end holdings list) and CalPERS (its Form 13F shares ÷ shares outstanding) are listed as pensions and sovereign funds: they are separate legal holders from the asset managers, though minor overlap is possible where an external manager runs part of a pension’s money. They are drawn in the bar only when every listed segment still fits within 100%. The rest is “all other shareholders”, with the company’s count of holders of record in its own words; that count understates owners, because shares held through a brokerage or fund are usually registered in a nominee’s name.
Caveats
“Everyone else” is 100% minus the leader and family. A holding reported as a share of one class only (for example “% of Class A”) is listed but never drawn in the bar or subtracted from everyone else. When a family or promoter-group total already includes the leader, the two are never added. A stake computed from a filing’s class counts is labelled “derived”, with the method shown.

Cash to shareholders

What it is
Cash dividends paid to the company’s own shareholders and cash spent buying back its shares, for one fiscal year.
Source
The cash-flow statement, often through the SEC’s XBRL data, re-checked by our validator.
Caveats
Buybacks pay whoever sells shares back to the company. Dividends to minority interests in subsidiaries are excluded.

Stock compensation

What it is
Share-based compensation expense across the whole company, and any broad employee share plan the filing describes.
Source
The notes to the financial statements.
Caveats
An accounting expense in the reporting currency, on a different basis from our pay estimate, so the two are shown side by side and never added.

Ecosystem

What it is
For platforms only: the company’s own measure of the volume that flows through it (gross merchandise volume, total payment volume, gross bookings and so on), in its own words and with its own definition, next to the revenue the platform keeps. Payouts to partners appear only when the filing reports them. Client assets are a balance, not a flow, so they are shown on their own.
Source
The 10-K, 20-F or annual report. Studies the company paid for are allowed only with the sponsor named, and are tagged “Company-commissioned”.
Why market value understates platforms
A platform’s market value reflects only the slice it keeps. The merchants, drivers, developers and creators who sell through it build their own businesses on the rest, and none of that shows up in the platform’s share price.
Caveats
Gross merchandise volume, payment volume and bookings are different measures, so we keep each company’s term. The rest of the volume is the value of the transactions, not anyone’s earnings. Volumes overlap across platforms and are never added.

Taxes

What it is
Cash income taxes paid during the fiscal year, net of refunds where the company reports it that way.
Source
The cash-flow statement’s supplemental disclosures or the tax note; for SEC filers, the XBRL fact for income taxes paid.
Caveats
Income taxes only. Payroll, sales, property and other taxes, and taxes collected on behalf of governments, are not included, so the figure understates what a company pays and collects.

R&D

What it is
Research and development expense for the fiscal year.
Source
The income statement or its notes; for SEC filers, the XBRL research and development fact.
Caveats
It measures spending, not what the research is worth. Banks, retailers and others often report none; we say so rather than estimate.

Where sales come from

What it is
Revenue by geography exactly as the company reports it, with its own region names.
Source
The segment or revenue note in the annual report.
Caveats
Companies draw regions differently, so shares aren’t comparable across companies. Globes show selected locations; employment and pay cover people worldwide. Amazon adds net sales by market, U.S. state investment, jobs and estimated GDP contributions, and selected facilities. Geography: Natural Earth; U.S. states: Census Bureau via US Atlas.

Footprint: where each company creates value

What it is
What a company itself publishes about where it operates: stores, plants, branches, employees, investment, taxes or estimated economic contribution, by U.S. state, by country or region, and its own description of its main sites. Each company’s measures are its own and keep its own names and definitions.
Source
The company’s filing (10-K Item 2 property tables, annual reports), its own impact reports and state or country pages, studies it commissioned, and regulators’ data about it (for banks, the FDIC’s branch and deposit data). Every row carries a verbatim quote, and a row is shown only when its source has passed our quote check.
Caveats
Dates differ by company and sometimes by state; each map shows its period, and figures before 2023 are tagged as older data. State totals are sums of the reported state figures; rates and shares are never summed, and country figures are never added into a world total, because regions and territories can overlap. Economic contribution estimates are the company’s own models, not measured output. Site pins mark the state or country a site is in, not its exact location. Country shapes and centroids: Natural Earth.

Net worth (third-party estimate)

What it is
An estimate of the leader’s personal wealth, shown in small type under “Their stake” at the top of each profile. It is a third-party estimate, not a company filing, and is tagged “Third-party estimate”.
Source
The list each profile names. Each profile links the publisher’s own data and quotes the entry verbatim.
Caveats
The publisher’s estimate at one date, which moves with share prices. Some entries are a family’s fortune; those read “Net worth (with family)”. Leaders who have died or aren’t on the list show no line. It is never added to value created, to their stake or to any other lens.

Evidence tiers

Every figure in a profile’s “How we got these numbers” list carries one of these tags.

Filing From the 10-K/annual report
Read in the company’s own filing (10-K, 20-F, 40-F, annual report, proxy statement, 13D/13G or an exchange disclosure), hosted by the SEC, the company, the exchange or the regulator. Each comes with a verbatim quote. Mirrors, news and data aggregators are never accepted.
Derived from filings
Computed from figures in filings, such as a stake from the share counts of two classes. The method is shown next to the figure.
Company-commissioned
A study the company paid for. It is labelled with its sponsor and publisher, and kept apart from filed figures.
Company-published
The company’s own website, impact report or state and country pages, outside its formal filings. Used for footprints: what a company says about where it operates.
Regulator data
Government data about the company, such as the FDIC’s Summary of Deposits for a bank’s branches and deposits by state.
Market data
A third-party market data source: CompaniesMarketCap for market value, and Stock Analysis for some employee counts.
Third-party estimate
An estimate published by someone other than the company, such as a net-worth list. Named with its publisher and date, and never treated as a filed figure.
Our estimate
Our own calculation, with its inputs shown. Only estimated pay is in this tier.

Figures that cite the SEC’s XBRL data are re-checked against it by our validator. Each source’s quote has also been checked against its document, and a figure whose source didn’t pass is left out rather than shown.

What we don’t count, and why

Consumer surplus
The value customers get beyond what they pay is real, and for many of these companies it is likely the largest share of all. Nobody measures it company by company, so we don’t put a number on it.
Ecosystem overlaps
A sale on one platform may be paid through another and shipped by a third. Each company’s volume is shown on its own and never added across companies.
Costs that fall on others
This list measures value created. It is not a full social ledger, and it doesn’t subtract costs a company may place on others.

Coverage

Which lenses each profile shows today, with the number of sourced figures behind each (for Footprint, each place figure and each site). Every profile also shows market value, people employed and estimated pay. Each link opens the profile at its lenses.
